The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Axworthy that Bill C-115, to establish a national program for occupational training, be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-115, to establish a national program for occupational training, with a certain amount of satisfaction. I guess everyone who sees the fruits of his or her labour suddenly arrive in some form of a legislation has a feeling of satisfaction, as I do today.
For a moment I should like to discuss the work of a task force which was chaired by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand). Six of my colleagues in the House of Commons were members of the task force, one of whom, due to sudden death, is no longer with us. We miss Bruce Lonsdale around here immensely. The seven of us got along well. We travelled the country from coast to coast over a period of approximately 12 months. We sat down to write a report which took a couple of months.
The report of the Special Committee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s ended up producing 186 recommendations, of which there were only minority reports written on three or four. This shows most graphically how well we got along, how we co-operated, and how we saw the problems associated with manpower training and a whole scope of issues once we got out there and experienced them first hand. I congratulate the government for setting up the task force. Some task forces have been more productive than others, but I think some very, very useful information has come out of every one of them. I think the minister will agree with me that Bill C-115 is the result of this task force and others which he had set up within his ministry. He may comment on that later.
National Training Act
There are a number of task force recommendations which are embodied in Bill C-115. The feeling, I suggest, is very similar to being a father; you experience the thrill of seeing something born after working so hard at it for so long a period of time.
I rise this afternoon with a good feeling in my heart. Now that we have Bill C-115 which does encompass certain recommendations from the committee, I hope that the minister will now convene the committee again for a meeting with himself in order that we may discuss some of our recommendations which have not yet been considered. Since the report was filed last October we have not had the opportunity to discuss with the minister which recommendations he does not favour and which ones he may be working on at the present time. Obviously, we know the ones which he favours because he has implemented them. However, I think a follow-up meeting is important because we hear the criticism from people time and time again that a matter is being studied and it will only result in another report which will end up on the shelf. We do not want that to happen.
We would like to see similar action taken to that taken by the task force on the handicapped and their follow-up on the Obstacles report. I would like to suggest to the minister today that he return with a counter report in order to reveal what has been accomplished, what is being considered and what has been rejected. That would be a very postive gesture on his part.
My colleague the hon. member from Rosedale (Mr. Crom-bie) mentioned the legislation process earlier and how well this particular process worked. There were a number of factors which arose from the process. We had a small committee which was comprised of members who were very knowledgeable on the subject we were discussing. No one was there to protect the government's rear flank or with any other similar motive. Our purpose was to attempt to reach a common goal. That process, I believe, could be used in many other areas. For instance, I see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) sitting in the House. I believe that when he is dealing with housing issues he should take a lesson from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). The graphic example given to us by that minister was very important.
While I say this with all kindness, I am not quite sure what happened to the minister's point of view between Tuesday's meeting and Thursday's meeting. My first concern in committee was co-operation with the provinces. On Tuesday the minister said that too often they-meaning the provinces- approach it as a one-way street: we co-operate and consult, and they simply decide. He went on to make a number of statements as to why certain provisions could not be put in the bill to assure co-operation with the provinces. One concerned the discussion of veto in course content and the construction of certain buildings within provinces that the federal government might fund. He summed it up to us on Tuesday by saying:

June 22, 1982
National Training Act
That is why I would not want to give a veto to any one of those segments and say that we are the only body in the country, as a national government, that can represent a national point of view.
The minister changed his mind some time between Tuesday and Thursday. To his credit, on Thursday he accepted a number of amendments that did allow vetos for provincial governments on certain aspects of the bill.
The hon. Dr. Bette Stephenson, who represented nine provinces, the territories and the Yukon, made a very strong plea for co-operative federalism. I believe that her presentation and her ideas probably exemplify what we on this side of the House would like to see happen to federal-provincial relations. Consultation with the provinces is now provided for in the legislation. It is assured that provinces will be given the opportunity to veto certain matters, although they do not have to do it. This is true for all provinces, including the one which unfortunately was not represented by Dr. Stephenson.
The absence of representations by Quebec was a grave disappointment to me. Although I am an Ontario member, I am very concerned about my sister province of Quebec and the attitude that government takes toward participation in matters such as these. Our committee spent a considerable amount of time conducting hearings in Quebec. We visited Chicoutimi, Jonquiere, Quebec City and Montreal. We had what I consider to be excellent representations by people representing the workplace, academics and the unions from that province. I believe that their concerns and thoughts were embodied in our report as much as any others. I found it extremely unfortunate for the Quebec minister to refuse absolutely to participate or co-operate with the other provinces in relating his concerns and improving our report. I, too, saw a very long telegram from the minister from Quebec, Mr. Marois, which did not offer any concrete changes to the act, and that concerned me. I suggested to the committee that we ask him to appear before us with his proposals. While he did not appear-in all fairness to him the invitation was not extended specifically to him-I am sorry that he did not co-operate on this bill because I believe it will benefit the workers in Quebec as much as the workers in the other nine provinces and the territories in Canada.
Another concern I had was over the consultation process with the private sector. One of our report's very strong recommendations was the use of the national labour market institute. It was a vehicle which would allow the private sector to become involved in the decision-making and informationgathering process.
Once we began our trips across Canada we became concerned when we quickly discovered that there was inaccurate information as to what is happening and what will happen in the marketplace. There was a complete lack of statistics and information. We were dealing with old statistics that had absolutely no further relevance to the conditions of the '80s. We believed that a national labour market institute which tied in business, labour, the large and small entrepreneur and the special needs groups, could provide the necessary information
as one of its functions to make reasonable and proper decisions on how training should be implemented in Canada.
My colleague from Rosedale spoke earlier about the amendment he introduced in order to insert the institute into the legislation. With the amendment that was accepted today by the government, we do have the framework for that. While we are somewhat concerned about iron-clad and firm commitments from that side of the House, we do have the commitment from the minister, which he made in committee, that he and his officials will work very diligently to set up this type of vehicle. It may not be exactly what the CLC wants, or what we proposed in the task force, but it will be something similar which will provide the necessary information in order for the minister and his officials to make reasonable decisions.
Something I would like to make very clear, and I think the minister will agree with this, is that we were somewhat preoccupied during committee with the issue of apprenticeships as if it only applied to apprenticeship training. I believe it should be made clear that while part of this bill does affect apprenticeship, there is other training required in Canada for very highly technical skills that may not be of apprenticeship nature but which nevertheless is required for the use of new equipment which is being installed in offices every day. We need people who are able to maintain that equipment. Technicians are sadly lacking in Canada today. We want to make it very clear that this bill covers training of a very wide scope, but training which is required in today's marketplace. I think someone said that for far too long the Ministry of Employment and Immigration has been training too many barbers and hairdressers, more barbers and hairdressers than there are heads of hair to cut in this country. I think that points out the problem we have been experiencing. It has obviously been recognized by the government in appointing this task force and also by this bill, and I am pleased to see that.
The apprenticeship program in Canada is sadly lacking. We found that in Germany, for example, 90 per cent of the manufacturing industries train people. In Britain, about 75 per cent are involved in training. In Canada we found from testimony that 20 per cent train in Canada. That was as near as we could figure because information is hard to get. People like to compare the European apprenticeship programs with the Canadian apprenticeship situation, but that cannot be done. Because of our split jurisdictions on various aspects, provinces have jurisdiction over education and that has been confirmed in the new Constitution. Other countries do not have those problems. I think that is the first point.
The second point is that we found that young people in European countries who sign on for apprenticeship finish that apprenticeship. It is like going to school. They are assured that they will finish that apprenticeship if they pass all the way along. They are not guaranteed jobs at the end, but they are assured of that apprenticeship and that if there is a slight slowdown in the industry, the apprentices are not the first to go. They are guaranteed that they will finish their course
June 22, 1982

unless, of course, there is a complete disaster. The negotiated agreements with their unions indicate that. I think that is very important.
1 would encourage labour in Canada to take a very long and hard look at that type of program because I am concerned that apprenticeship programs are on for a few months and then they are off. In these economic times, there is no question but that it is the apprentices who are being laid off first and are missing out on that much-needed education. So I appeal to the ministry, to the minister, to labour and to management to get together and take a long, hard look at our apprenticeship programs in this country and see whether we are doing the right thing. We should take a look at the modular educational process as opposed to the old process of four years of apprenticeship, because I think that maybe those days have gone.
Finally, as my colleague from Rosedale did, I want to congratulate a few people. It is always good for young people like us, rookies in the House, to watch an old pro at work, if I can use that terminology and it is not unparliamentary. As everyone in this House and many people in Canada know, for a great many years the hon. member for Brandon-Souris and his wife have diligently worked for those less fortunate than the rest of us. He was on the task force on the handicapped and he came to that committee with one purpose in mind-to ensure that those people with special needs were included in Bill C-115. Like a tenacious little terrier who has got hold of someone's pantleg, he would not let go until he had finished the deed. I want to congratulate him and thank him very much for teaching we rookies how to get the job done, an important job done.
To my colleagues, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) and the hon. member for Rosedale, who served on the committee and also spent a great deal of time in the committee, I say thank you. To the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bujold), and to the staff who were most co-operative with us, I also want to say thank you.
I think I had only one disappointment in the whole process. That was that those people who served on the task force really did not show up in the committee, with the exception of the chairman, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East, who just showed up for one of the meetings. I was disappointed that they were not there to help put forward the points that we were trying to make to encourage the minister to bring in the amendments and to produce a good bill. I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) will be following me. He was on the Employment Opportunities for the '80s committee. He did not show up, but he had some changed responsibilities and had good reason not to be there. That was a disappointment.
Now we face the challenge. Now we have the training bill in place. Now we must start training people. But, more importantly, we must train them for jobs which are available in the eighties. Right now those jobs are lacking, with one and a half million people unemployed. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has disappointed us for two and a half years. 1 hope and pray that on Monday night he will come in with a
National Training Act
very positive, very upbeat, very inspirational type of budget which will get the economy back on its feet and give faith to the Canadian people who have lost their trust in the Canadian government, so they can be assured that when they invest, their investments will be good and so we can provide the jobs that are needed. Now that we have this training bill in place, I urge the minister to get on with the job of training.

Mr. Speaker, as indicated by the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid), I was spokesman for our party on questions of employment for a number of years. I served with hon. members from the other parties on the parliamentary task force which looked at the question of employment for the eighties. I was then assigned different responsibilities. Therefore, I was not really able to participate in the work of the standing committee which considered this bill, but I closely followed its work and its recommendations.
I want to say, as did my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper), who is now our spokesman on employment matters, that we will vote for this bill. We will do it despite the fact that we have some serious doubts about the government's programs or the ability of this bill to do a much better job than has been done in the past. I want to remind members of the committee that when the head of the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen was before the parliamentary task force, he referred to the present department of employment and its ability to do the job it is supposed to do. While I may not quote him exactly, 1 am certain that I will relate the spirit of what he had to say. As I remember, he said that if an employer is looking for a good, skilled employee to fill a vacancy in his plant, the last place he would go would be to the department of employment. I think that is a very serious indictment of the department.
Let me deal with what I consider to be some of the major difficulties, not only with the act but also with the government's approach to the problem of unemployment. It is pretty obvious to me that the major proposals contained in this bill were drafted some considerable time ago, a time when the depth and severity of the depression we are presently in was not expected by the government. I say "depression" in all seriousness because I think it is much more than a recession.
As usual, the government received incorrect and bad advice from its senior economic advisers. According to official statistics from Statistics Canada, we now have one and a quarter million unemployed. We all know that there are probably another 300,000 or 400,000 people who are also unemployed, but Statistics Canada only counts as unemployed those who are actively looking for work.
Today's Financial Times highlighted the severity of the problem with a front page story headlined "UIC rates set for huge rise". I will read into the record a couple of paragraphs indicating its predictions. It states:
Some private forecasters now believe that the total bill for unemployment insurance benefits in 1982 will be at least $7 billion to $8 billion, maybe higher if the unemployment rate continues to rise. This is a huge increase over the $4.8

June 22, 1982
National Training Act
billion in benefits paid out last year. And it means the account will face a deficit by year-end of at least $2 billion-ten times more than the $218 million shortfall originally planned.
It goes on to indicate the very sharp increase in unemployment insurance premiums which will be required to be paid next year by both employees and employers. As I see it, even if the programs to be implemented under the provisions of this bill succeed, which I doubt for reasons that I will indicate later, we will simply have a much better trained large group of unemployed.
The bill was obviously prepared before the failure of the megaprojects became apparent. The failure of these projects on which the federal government's whole job strategy was based considerably modifies the employment situation in Canada.
In his address to the Canadian Information Processing Society in Saskatoon in May of this year, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) mentioned the strong position of Canada due to the resource industries in the west. It is clear in this speech that he considered that developing of skills required by these industries where they were located constituted a crucial aspect of the whole national training program.
The picture today is, of course, totally different. Today the unemployment rate is over 10 per cent. Those who are unemployed are no longer only the unskilled workers. In the past year vacancies for accountants, executives, engineers, scientists and other professionals decreased by more than 47 per cent. It is reported now that university graduates are faced with increasing difficulties in finding jobs.
The petrochemical industry and the forestry and manufacturing sectors are among the hardest hit. The financial sector opportunities for university graduates also appear to be limited. Under these circumstances, it seems to be clear that any program to improve the employment situation in Canada should be placed within a broader strategy and a stronger commitment to full employment.
We know that the parliamentary task force on employment in the eighties, which unfortunately the minister did not pay much attention to, said that the goal of the Canadian government should be full employment. It defined full employment as 96 per cent of the work force employed and only 4 per cent unemployed. As I have indicated, we now have 10 per cent of the work force unemployed.
It would be impossible to carry out job creation and training programs which would be of any real benefit given this situation. This prediction of the parliamentary task force is in contrast to the departmental task force headed by Dr. Dodge which ignored that advice, unfortunately and so was not followed by the minister. The Dodge report overlooked completely the whole question of unemployment in this country.
Another principle underlying the bill before us is the perception of labour market planning simply as a problem of matching workers to jobs. The bill reflects no attempt to situate employment planning in the wider context of planning of the whole economic activity. For example, in his Saskatoon speech
the minister maintained that the service sectors will continue to be improved in employment creation, that growth will no longer be centred in the health and educational fields but rather in the business and computer-related services.
This is an end result of the government policy rather than a natural development. Moreover, it is not at all clear whether it is a desirable development, given the unsatisfactory performance we now have in health and education services and given the fact that the more we computerize, the more people, particularly women in the traditional fields in which they work, will be out of work. There is no indication in the provisions of this bill or in any of the speeches made by the minister that the serious inequities which now exist in the field of employment for women have been considered at all or that they will be improved in a meaningful way after this bill is enacted.
Let me illustrate briefly what I mean by this claim which I have just made. Women are under-represented in manpower training courses. In 1979, women represented 39 per cent of the employed labour force, 46 per cent of the unemployed labour force and 51 per cent of the source population. Yet in 1979-80, female participation in full-time institutional training programs was only 33 per cent.
In the industrial training courses, the percentage of women participants declined from the 1978-79 figure of 29 per cent to 27.4 per cent. Worse, women comprise only 3 per cent of the apprenticeship training program, a rate which has remained constant for the last ten years. This is despite the previous claims of the minister that the government is giving serious consideration to ways to improve the situation for women in these non-traditional fields.
Occupational segregation of women starts with manpower and its department. The inequities of women's occupations in the labour force have been well documented. Sixty per cent of all working women work at three kinds of jobs: clerical, sales and service. These jobs are typically low-paying, dead-end jobs requiring few skills. Rather than becoming an instrument of change, manpower training programs initiate and encourage ghettoization. In 1979-80, 93 per cent of all manpower trainees enrolled in clerical and related institutional training courses were women. Clerical and related courses ranked first as a specialty for women in industrial training courses as well.
The CEC counsellors, who are the first entry to the system, are the first barrier to women doing better. The individual CEC counsellor has almost total control in the selection of programs for women. They overwhelmingly stream women into traditional occupations. The counsellors are not only hampered by personal biases and attitudes; the majority are further handicapped by a lack of formal training in job counselling. Furthermore, counsellors often lack comprehensive knowledge of the range of courses available to their women clients.
Essentially, the counsellors do not work as career planners
but perceive training as an end rather than a means. In effect,
June 22, 1982

women are often streamed into short-term training programs to eliminate their numbers from the unemployment rolls because CEC counsellors are under tremendous pressure to process clients as quickly and as cheaply as possible.
I now wish to comment on wage subsidy programs. In 1978, 75 per cent of the wage subsidies went to small, non-union firms with 20 or less employees. In these small firms, women run the risk of becoming a cheap source of labour, vulnerable to lay-offs and unemployment. In 1975, three months after women completed their training in a non-traditional occupation, it was found that they earned $67 less than men with identical characteristics in similar occupations.
Since the department does only a limited three-month follow-up of its trainees in the wage subsidy program, it is difficult to determine if women are retained as permanent employees in any significant numbers. Without long-term monitoring and evaluation of the career paths of these women trainees, it is difficult to assess if they are promoted in any significant numbers from their entry level positions.
By creating a policy which subsidizes small firms for accepting female trainees and by slotting 10 to 15 per cent of the non-traditional instutional training seats for women, the goal of promoting women into better-paying industries and jobs that have been traditionally dominated by men is not being satisfied.
The government and the minister have rejected the principles enunciated in the parliamentary task force of contract compliance and affirmative action. I will talk about those in a few minutes. The national training program of the government reflects the government's response mainly to the Dodge report to which 1 have already referred.
Virtually, Mr. Speaker, the minister has rejected most of the important recommendations made by the parliamentary task force, a task force of which the majority of its members come from the Liberal majority of this Parliament. It is a task force whose recommendations were, as the member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) said, almost all unanimous, yet most of the recommendations of that parliamentary task force were ignored and rejected by the minister. We see that in this proposal with regard to the National Training Act.
Let me indicate some of the proposals which were in effect rejected by the government. The parliamentary task force was told repeatedly by representatives of labour, industry, educators and by community groups that until now employers, with very few exceptions, have not trained the skilled workers they need. They have been content to import skilled workers from overseas or to steal skilled workers from other employers.
There is no proof at all, Mr. Speaker, that employers will do better as long as they are not required to train by law or by regulation. Voluntary efforts, or the kind of give-aways and bribes which the minister proposes the government follow, will be a failure as they have been in the past. I will deal with that a little later.
National Training Act
Let me deal with three or four of the specific recommendations which the parliamentary task force made and which have been rejected and ignored by the government. The parliamentary task force pointed out that 28.4 per cent of Canadians are functionally illiterate. Mr. Speaker, that is almost a record and a record of which we ought to be ashamed before any of the modern industrialized countries of the western world.
The parliamentary task force recommended that a special effort would have to be made to prepare these people for higher skills-training. There is no sign of that in the bill or in anything the minister has said.
My colleague mentioned earlier that the parliamentary task force recommended a ten-year crash program, operated jointly by the three levels of government. The parliamentary task force pointed out that women, natives and the handicapped are underrepresented in the skilled trades and professions. It said that the government should reaffirm its commitment to eradicate functional illiteracy and should introduce an affirmative action program and a program of contractual compliance for an increase in the training of women, natives, the handicapped, and other minority groups. It recommended that there should be an Indian economic and employment strategy, together with an Indian educational training strategy, to be developed by Indians. There is no sign of that, Mr. Speaker.
This bill is based on recommendations made by that internal task force, of the employment department, headed by Mr. Dodge. It did not do what the parliamentary task force did; it did not go across the country listening to groups from one end of the country to the other. It met with a few bureaucrats in the department, and probably with a few bureaucrats in some of the provincial departments, and made its recommendations.
The recommendations made by the Dodge task force which are embodied in this bill were supported to a large extent by the private sector. It was received with suspicion and is under a great deal of suspicion by trade unions and by provincial governments. Provincial governments, however, realizing the power and the financial ability of the federal government to fund programs, even if they are not completely satisfied with them, have had to go along with the proposals of the government.
The trade unions are concerned by the very limited role assigned to them under this program. They have also pointed out that there is an increasingly large role to be played by the employers in providing training. The unions, however, feel, with the vast experience they have, that the on-the-job training has been quite unsatisfactory, as did most employers, educators and community groups that came before the parliamentary task force. This raises doubts as to the effectiveness of training programs left to the initiative of employers.
I would point out today, Mr. Speaker, as I have in the past, that the particular agreements for training which the minister has made with various industry groups were made without consultation with the unions in those industries. Such programs are thus likely to be essentially generous subsidies to the private sector, which do not and will not make a significant

June 22, 1982
National Training Act
contribution towards the solution of the country's employment problems.
As an alternative, the Canadian Labour Congress suggested a grant-levy system, to be administered by a training board composed equally of representatives of trade unions and management. The board would have had authority to set a levy for all employers in their sector to cover (a) the administrative expenses of the board, (b) the training program, (c) the research of the board and (d) grants to employers.
All employers in the sector would pay the levy set by the board. Then the employers who actually provide training according to the standard set by the board would receive a grant to offset all or part of the cost of training. If a firm does more than its share of training, it could receive more back in grants than it had paid in the levy. This system would provide both an incentive and a penalty, and would thus persuade employers to train. That is an objective which it is very difficult to attain without such a mechanism of enforcement.
The parliamentary task force did not accept that proposal of the Canadian Labour Congress, but it did bring forward an alternative. Under the alternative, employers would have had to pay in a different form for training, whether they did it or not, and would be compensated if they trained their workers. That recommendation of the parliamentary task force was, in effect, rejected by the government.
The task force report was prepared and adopted without consultation with unions or other groups. The suggestions of the CLC were not taken into account by the minister or his department. Like the labour unions, the provinces too were dissatisfied with the increasing role given to the private sector in the training programs.
At present, the balance of the institutional industrial training is 85 per cent to institutions and 15 per cent to industrial training. In 1980-81, $656 million, out of a total expenditure of $770 million, federal training dollars, were channelled through provincial educational institutions. The switch of training funds to the private sector, which is to be given more encouragement to train workers, means that the provinces will have their funds cut by up to 10 per cent this year. Like the labour unions, the provinces have expressed their concern about reliance for training programs on the voluntary compliance of the private sector and the lack of explicit mention of governmental action which might be necessary in the absence of this voluntary compliance. This point was expressed very forcefully by the Ontario ministry.
The provinces have also mentioned that the program might lead to a situation where already available services are duplicated. It has every reason to be suspicious about the ability of the department to deliver the kind of programs that they talk about. We know from bitter experience how wrong the department has been in past years.
Finally, they raise doubts as to the ability of the federal government to forecast accurately what skills will be in demand in future. Given previous federal failures in certain areas-and I refer to the forward occupational imbalance
listing, which was ignored by industry for planning purposes, and the Canadian occupational forecasting program, which was judged not very useful by local CEIC centres-the forecasting ability of the Canadian occupational projection system, or COPS, as it is known, a major component of the training program, remains an important provincial worry.
Apart from these issues raised by the concerned parties, there are important problems related to the principle underlying the National Training Act about which I have very serious doubts. Let me deal with some specific shortcomings that I see in the government's program. There is a need to train thousands who lack basic education, to which I have already referred is deficient. It means that they are not now able to get the kind of training that is or may be available for those skilled jobs for which there is or may be a demand. In other words, Mr. Speaker, even if we have the right training programs, a very large percentage of the Canadian people would not and do not have the education to qualify to take that training opportunity which would be available. I have already spoken about the large number of Canadians who are functionally illiterate.
The parliamentary task force recommended that we adopt the national right to read program operated by the federal and provincial governments together with private and voluntary organizations. There would be a need for a major increase in funds for such programs, to provide the basic training for skill development. What we have actually seen in recent years, however, were substantial cutbacks in these programs rather than the increases which the task force and other groups indicated were needed.
We have failed to deal with the needs of special groups. The government has rejected any real commitment to the use of affirmative action programs to provide employment opportunities to minority groups, which include women, natives, the handicapped and new immigrants, so that such people can take their place in our modern society. Even if training were provided for these groups, if employment is not assured then the training would be self-defeating in a period of high unemployment. At this time, when there are so many people unemployed, it would be much easier for employers, both public and private, to find work for the many middle-class men and women who wish to work rather than for natives or immigrants who would require longer and more expensive assistance to find and keep meaningful work. Unless we help them they will be permanently forced into low paid, unskilled, dirty work, or onto the welfare rolls of our cities.
The record of government departments in hiring native people is poor, almost without exception. The government's supposed commitment to affirmative action will not be realized unless these programs are given teeth, and senior administrators are given the responsibility of delivering specific goals by specific dates. There are signs that this is taking place.
There are jobs for these minority groups. We need native
teachers, we need native social workers and health workers,

June 22, 1982
building maintenance people, and resource officers, as well as prison workers. We need them on the reserves and we need them in the cities to which they are moving in increasing numbers. The government and the department have failed completely to face up to the problem of these people as they have refused to face up to so many problems for which they have responsibility.
We see these shortcomings. We are not too hopeful that the bill will do a better job than the old act, or that the government will do more than it did in the past. This new measure is better than none, however, and so we will vote for the bill although, to say the least, reluctantly.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have a few short comments to make on this bill. I know we have a royal assent at 5.45, and that the minister also wants to say a few words, so I shall be very brief. Nevertheless, I would like to add my own words to other comments made in this House regarding the exceptional efforts made by my colleague from Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) in his word on amendments to this bill. It would seem that the legislation has been vastly improved as a result of amendments that were accepted after prior discussion in committee.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, as a member for Quebec, I am once again far from happy to see that nine provinces plus the Northwest Territories have agreed and that Quebec is not a part of this general agreement. Granted, the amendments give the provinces some increased powers, but as a result of these amendments, the provinces will also have to take the blame for turning down certain federal proposals.
1 had hoped, and I pointed this out in committee to the minister responsible, that the Quebec minister's request to have a discussion before the bill was passed would be met. I did the best I could to make the minister understand, after his very pertinent remarks to the committee, that it was important for him to meet the Quebec minister, considering the comments sent by telegram to the minister and a number of members. I felt, and I will feel, that it is vital that the two ministers should meet. I know, and the minister certainly has many possibilities, that he would be willing to try to show some flexibility if such a request were made. He was finally advised not to meet the Quebec minister on this subject, and that is probably why Quebec is not part of this agreement. It is unfortunate, and I truly regret this fact. It also puts me in a rather difficult position in relation to other members, because of their comments and the agreements between various provinces, and I wish I could be as pleased as my colleagues are about the fact that their provinces have agreed to co-operate with the federal government on this legislation.
That is not the case, however, and since the minister did not make the special effort he could have made, Mr. Speaker, I find the whole situation most unfortunate and regrettable. I know, people are going to tell me that amendments will make
National Training Act
it possible for Quebec as well as all the other provinces to have a say in this kind of consultation, but the fact remains that proposals will be initiated by the federal government, and that is the kind of unilateralism we have often criticized. This reminds me of other subjects and conflicts we have witnessed here in the House of Commons, in which the federal government unilaterally maintained its proposals and let the provinces take the blame for failing to agree or co-operate. Much has been said about consultation, and the minister has tried to convince us that there would be real consultation, but, Mr. Speaker, experience has shown that consultation is not always enough. I would have preferred agreements, and in view of the very positive arguments put forward by the minister, and the objectives of this legislation, it seems to me it should have been possible to convince ten, and not only nine provinces. Of course, there will be those who say that today, nothing can be done with the government of Quebec. I can assure the House that previous governments under Mr. Bourassa and Mr. Johson were just as demanding with respect to occupational training as the present government of Quebec. It is always useful to remember Quebec's history.
I have just a short comment to remind the minister of one of the recommendations of the Pepin-Robarts report. In fact, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) was the right person to remind the minister responsible that the report contains a recommendation which demands recognition for the distinctive position of Quebec, compared with the other provinces, a recommendation that was not drafted by the separatists but by federalist Tories and Grits, among them the Minister of Transport who is a member of the cabinet. If the Minister of Transport had wanted to show the slightest bit of good faith, he could have reminded the minister that this distinctiveness should be reflected in the proposals being made today by the federal government. Today, this distinctiveness has been totally ignored in the bill now before the House. 1 repeat, Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see that nine provinces have approved the principle of this bill and are prepared to cooperate with the minister in this area. However, I find it most regrettable that the government failed to obtain Quebec's cooperation, and I am convinced not enough has been done, and to prove it-

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the gesture. There are many things I could say about this bill. The fact that it has taken us close to two years to achieve this major change in training is one. Perhaps I could just indicate to hon. members that this will provide, in what has been a very long session, one of the most important gestures this Parliament can make toward those Canadians who are looking to their future in the job market. It will give them some hope and ambition, and confidence that the future can be theirs because they will have better training.
It means that we will be able to offer well over $1 billion in expenditures for new training to over 250,000 Canadians. It means there are special measures for women to go into nontraditional work. There are special measures to encourage employers to hire native people and those with disabilities. There are major efforts to provide every province, and employers and unions across Canada, with the ability to build new training facilities, new equipment and new laboratories to expand our training system across Canada substantively.
This is a very major moment for this Parliament, Mr. Speaker, and it is not, as members opposite have said, the product of one or two people; it is the product of many people.
It started with the task force, and contrary to the impression the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) tried to leave, it was very much based on the recommendations of that task force which was composed of members from all sides. There were a lot of very diligent and loyal officials of this government who spent literally hundreds of thousands of hour working to bring about a training program. There was the cooperation of many provincial officials who worked with us in two federal-provincial conferences to bring this about.
I would point out to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) that the lack of participation by the Quebec minister is not our fault. He did not come to those conferences, even though he was invited; he did not prepare recommendations, even though he was asked; he did not offer any suggestions, even though the invitation was given.

It is not true that the government of Quebec wishes to cooperate with the federal government, but I hope to reach an agreement with the government of Quebec quite soon, although the latter will have to declare its intentions with respect to this agreement.

So, Mr. Speaker, there are many people involved, and 1 want to pay tribute in particular to my parliamentary secretary who was responsible for guiding this bill through the labyrinth of Parliament and obtaining co-operation from everyone concerned. I also want to pay tribute in particular to members of the committee. We worked very closely together over the past two weeks to arrive at what I think is a good bill which will serve Canadians in the future.
We can now go to young people, natives, women, the workers of this country, and say we have a framework of training which gives them some hope and confidence that the skills they need for the new workplace can be theirs. But we will have to continue this spirit of co-operation. I hope members on both sides will continue to work with me and my department as we take this legislation and turn it into reality so that we can deal with these difficult economic problems of our times, and provide a real sense of purpose and direction for the workplace of the future. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, as we await the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod I want to resume my comments on Bill C-92 by indicating to my colleagues that I had just finished reminding the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) that among the issues with which we are concerned with respect to ports legislation is the capacity of the central Crown corporation involved to act in the role of banker. How this would happen, its desirability, was spelled out in background papers which were widely discussed in
Canada Ports Corporation Act
Canada and which emanated from the ministry. I had indicated to the House that we were somewhat disappointed, to say the least, to find that those provisions were not carried through in the bill. I indicated, and I reiterate now, that those are provisions we will at least hope to see when the matter is finally before us in committee.
There are some other aspects of the bill that require further clarification. For instance, a port, as long as it is not a local port corporation, may be allowed to change its status to a harbour commission, providing for even further autonomy.
A local port corporation in order to achieve that would in effect have to disband itself and then apply for harbour commission status. I do not believe, nor did I understand, that that was to be the intent of the minister or his officials in the drafting of this legislation. Regretfully that is the situation within the bill itself. Our concern, of course, is that we do not believe that any port should have to suffer through that much red tape in order to change its status.
With respect to local port corporations, and again this hinges on the local autonomy issue-the degree of autonomy that will be extended to local port corporations under this legislation-why is it just the Canada Ports Corporation that would be allowed to petition the minister for establishment of a local port corporation? If one of the criteria for the establishment of a local port corporation is that of local interest, then why can the local community not be allowed to petition the transport minister? Would this not be further proof of the need for a local port corporation if the local community itself were able to participate directly.
Another criterion for the establishment of a local port corporation is that of financial self-sufficiency. What is the definition of financial self-sufficiency? Will it differ from one port to the other? If it will not, then why is the Canada Port Corporation allowed to select and choose which statutory powers to give each local port corporation contained in the list of powers in Part II of the Act? These are questions for which we will be seeking detailed answers. Why should not all local port corporations be established with the same set of ground rules, and have equal and identical statutory powers? The act does not give as much guidance on that.
If one local port corporation will be allowed by the CPC to have more statutory powers because of its so-called financial self-sufficiency, does this mean that the CPC will have more stringent control over the local port corporation that does not have as many or as broad statutory authorities? I think this is a vital concern and I hope this discrepancy will be clarified and, more important, rectified in committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8:00 p.m.

The House resumed from June 14, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pepin that Bill C-92, an act to amend the National Harbours Board Act, the Government Harbours and Piers Act, the Harbour Commissions Act, the Canada Shipping Act and the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.

Mr. Speaker, when the distinguished Senate and her representatives, the Governor General in her presence in the Senate, summoned us to other business in Parliament, I had been talking about some of the concerns that we on this side have with respect to Bill C-92, the pending ports legislation.
In the time I have remaining I would like to put on the record some of the other concerns which we have about this bill. I would sum up what I have said up to this point, but
having had my speech interrupted three times already, I believe I will simply carry on. The minister is aware of some of our concerns, a few of which are being looked upon favourably by the minister. I believe when this matter goes to committee you will find a non-partisan committee such as the one which dealt with the bill we considered this afternoon. I believe you will find a committee which is prepared to work at rectifying some of the reservations we have about this bill. As I indicated at the outset, some of those concerns are critical and need to be assessed.
Another concern we have is that all of the local port corporations' board of directors are appointed by cabinet. Although the language in the bill has been made neater, it still in fact provides for a cabinet appointment on the recommendation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). While we may all love the present philosopher who occupies that high post, it is not always the case that this chamber can automatically have trust and confidence in the selection processes made by a minister with respect to appointments to these local boards.
To allay fears of some over-zealous, crass patronage, of which we have seen a lot recently-I would remind the minister of our former colleague, Jack Horner, going all the way to the top of CN. We do have to talk about Pierre Juneau and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We do not have to talk about Sylvia Ostry in OECD. We surely do not have to talk in this chamber about the brother-in-law team that we now have running VIA on the one hand and Canadian National on the other. That is nepotism in its worst form, and conflict of interest.
Jack Horner was your transport minister.
I know that he was. Tell me how you can avoid conflict of interest when brothers-in-law are running VIA Rail and CN?
Competence.
Competence in conflict. This country deserves better than that. Does the hon. member mean to tell me that there are not other people who could competently run VIA Rail?
Who?
If you sit in your chair I will entertain your question when I finish.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. I wonder if the hon. member agrees with me that Pierre Franche, before he was appointed to VIA Rail, was doing a very good job in all of the functions and appointments he received from the federal government. He is a well-qualified man. He received his qualifications from all over the world.

I will respond to that question. I come from the port of Halifax-Dartmouth, in Atlantic Canada. I suggest that he take a look at the money spent, if the hon. member

June 22, 1982

wants to join the debate, and tell me how it is fair. Of course Pierre Franche did well. He had S600 million to spend between Beauharnois and Quebec City. What did we have in Atlantic Canada in the same period? We had $40 million. Tell me how that equates. Surely he did a good job. Everyone in Montreal knows he did a good job and everyone in Quebec knows he did a good job, but he is damned outside of those two areas. Talk to the people on the west coast and on the east coast. He did not do a good job, and he will not do a good job with VIA Rail. He will have to prove it every step of the way. It is negativism, and the hon. member knows it, and it is nepotism of the worst kind.
We want to allay these fears, so all we are asking is that the minister consider, just consider, between now and the time this matter gets into committee, whether or not he might not extend the capacities extended under the Harbour Commissions Act, so that we might draw into this decision-making process labour and the municipalities. It is not that I necessarily want them or believe that they should necessarily be part of the local ports corporation, but they should be drawn into the recommendations and into the government's thought processes so that there will be belief and credibility in the names of the nominees placed before cabinet for these jobs. We want to allay the suspicion that these are nothing but pork barrel positions. I think it is time we did that. Knowing the minister, I am sure he will consider a formula which accommodates the capacity of the Harbour Commissions Act.
Also, will he at least consider making certain that his nominees at least live in the area of jurisdiction with respect to appointments? With respect to these 20 mini Crown corporations, we do not want to see boards of directors such as that found in the Canada Development Corporation. What is the analogy? This government puts its head office in Vancouver and a chairman, a chief executive officer, president of the board, in Toronto.
He does not live in Vancouver.

No, so we want to avoid that. It is humiliating, somewhat arrogant, and it did not serve that area well. So, assure us that the process will not be an insult to the local community.
In conclusion, I welcome this bill. Some of my colleagues have strong reservations with respect to it.
Misgivings.

They have some misgivings about it. But if there is one thing that I need to say tonight, it is that Canada needs this piece of legislation. It is not good legislation. It is not legislation in its best form. I believe the Standing Committee on Transport can improve it. I believe the minister has a sufficiently open mind that he will allow improvements. I think we can produce a good piece of legislation.
Canada Ports Corporation Act
We need more accountability. I will reiterate just one or two points. We want joint auditorship or sole auditorship by the Auditor General of Canada. That relates to accountability, and the reason we need or believe that we want that at this point in time is simply that we have not seen the government's intentions with respect to Crown corporations over the medium to long haul. In the absence of a white paper and in the absence of legislation dealing with Crown corporations in our system, in our structure, we have reservations and we believe them to be valid. In that context, we believe that accountability, credibility of accountability, can be enhanced or enriched if the minister will accede to an amendment which will allow the Auditor General to be either the auditor for the Canada Ports Corporation and the local ports corporations or at least joint auditor. Therefore, I ask him to consider that.
The second point that I would reiterate in closing relates to the perception of autonomy. The bill, at first reading and on first blush, does indicate some degree of autonomy. We still have to see all the bylaws. We have to see the borrowing powers. We have to see the degree to which ports are treated equitably with respect to their statutory obligations, regulations and so on, the things that give them life and make them work. But remember, Mr. Minister and Mr. Speaker, that the people in the port community in this nation and its users will be watching this piece of legislation. They will be watching it to see whether, in fact, it does extend autonomy, whether there is that individual capacity to move, to expand, to promote vigorously, and to develop and compete without extending to any one port an advantage over another port.
I refer to the comments of my hon. friend opposite about the chairman of the National Harbours Board. The harbours and ports in this country have not been dealt with equitably over the last 15 or 20 years. The minister knows that. I hope this bill will extend equal statutory authority to all ports which will enhance and enrich their capacity to compete vigorously with one another for offshore export trade and import trade. The legislation designed in the early 1930s, coming into law in the mid-1930s, surviving for 45 years, has in fact been an excellent piece of legislation. It has served this country well, but it is outdated and it must be changed. I give to the minister my undertaking to support him to the degree I can, here on the floor on second reading, in the committee and back on report stage and on third reading. All that we on this side ask is that he support us in trying to make this a piece of legislation which will last as long as did the legislation based on the work of Commissioner Gibbs in the 1930s.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to be the first to speak for our party on the ports bill, Bill C-92, an act to amend the National Harbours Board Act, the Government Harbours and Piers Act, the Harbour Commissions Act, the Canada Shipping Act and Recreational Harbours Act. As the Member of Parliament for the riding of Vancouver East, which borders on the Port of Vancouver, I have a very special interest in this bill. Over the past year, as

June 22, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
part of the planning process in which the minister invited us to participate, I have consulted with National Harbours Board officials, maritime unions, regional and neighbourhood planning bodies, city councillors and also community residents near the port to get their opinions and their reactions to the proposed change in Canada's port policy.
I might say that the minister who invited this kind of involvement process seems to have indeed ignored many of the suggestions which were put to him, at least those made from my part of the country. The intent of the bill and its main features involve the creation of autonomous local port corporations, which are expected to be financially self-sufficient, regional administration of the smaller harbours and ports in Canada, as well as the creation of consultative bodies which would advise on port planning. A new ports policy which would embody a decentralized approach to port management and administration of ports has long been requested in this country and has long been delayed. We on this side of the House will support this bill in principle, but we do have a number of concerns which will require amendments before we can vote for it.
I would like to briefly review some of the historical trends which are relevant to the bill before us today, that is, Bill C-92. The concept of local autonomy in ports was present early in our history, way back in the 1800s, in the administration of the Port of Montreal as well as other ports. By 1906, however, the Port of Montreal had become so badly managed that the local board of trade asked the federal government to revert to the original form of central control. We see a reversal of the process that we are talking about today.
Because of the difficulties that Canadian ports were experiencing, by 1932 it was requested that Sir Anthony Gibb, a British authority on ports, investigate the financial losses and the inefficiencies of the Canadian port system. His 1932 "National Ports Survey", as it was called, reported that the local harbours boards were riddled with patronage. That was a very important point that he made. It is very relevant today. We are riddled with patronage by the party in power. He said they did not have the financial resources to provide low transport charges required for Canadian trade, and they failed to represent local interests and port users. This is quite important. The criticisms by Mr. Gibb are particularly relevant to some of the proposed changes in Bill C-92.
In 1936 the National Harbours Act established a highly centralized national ports system for Canada. We then moved to the National Harbours Board structure. Policy decisions were made in Ottawa for some ports that in some cases were thousands of miles away. As ports developed and national trade expanded, a highly centralized system of control became much too restrictive. Of course, it was overly bureaucratic, with long delays in decisions needed for practical operation of the port. Operational decisions were delayed by communication problems between coastal ports located thousands of miles away from isolated Ottawa.
Most restrictive, of course, was the statutory ceiling on contracts which required Treasury Board approval for any expenditures over $50,000. In his remarks the minister referred to the quite unrealistic administrative restrictions which this resulted in. Also, rates were imposed centrally by a three-person National Harbours Board.
The Glassco commission of 1962-63 recommended decentralization of the federal government services. Remember, this was in 1962, over 20 years ago. At that time it concluded, "Time and considerable correspondence and expenses will be saved if the local office is given the authority to make its own decisions in all cases except those involving government policy". Twenty years ago we needed decentralization. The need for reform was established 20 years ago. Yet subsequent Liberal governments have continued to delay changes time and time again.
The continuing problems therefore and the increasing inadequacy of the centralized port system led to a Speech from the Throne in 1974 which promised a reorganization of Canada's system of port management.
In July, 1975, the Scott committee, an interdepartmental committee, recommended the establishment of a new, single comprehensive port organization based largely on a national ports policy, but with substantial local autonomy in the management of the local ports and regional participation in the port-planning process. Still no action was taken by the Liberal government.
In 1977, Bill C-6, an act respecting Canadian ports, was prepared. This was to reflect the considerations of the Glassco commission and the Scott commission to foster local port autonomy where this was of local interest and where a port was expected to be financially self-sufficient. Need I say this bill was not enacted. It is almost like a conspiracy to delay changes.
In the glorious days of 1979 when the Conservative Party came to power, the needs of Canadian ports remained the same. The then minister of transport proposed a very similar bill which, of course, went down the tube with the Conservative government.
Because the Conservative position on decentralization was similar to that of the Liberal government, and reflected strong pressure from all regions of Canada, I cannot understand why some members of the Conservative Party, and I believe some from my region of the country, are opposing this bill. They certainly do not reflect the desires of the city of Vancouver which has undertaken a major study of this legislation. 1 will quote some of their recommendations later.
The city of Vancouver has asked for quick passage despite some reservations which we hold and which we will insist should become amendments in committee. The greater Vancouver regional district also supports this legislation, again with some caution. It certainly is important that we act on this, but with the changes that are needed.
The complex trends and developments in recent years require a much more responsive and effective system of port management. These trends include an enormous increase in
June 22, 1982

economic development throughout the world, and an accompanying expansion of international trade. There has been a development of new multi-model systems for containerized cargo and larger size facilities. The 1973 energy crisis characterizing the OPEC decade greatly increased competition between ports. In addition, there are community demands for more sensitive, integrated and responsive approaches to planning and, I might say, more control over safety and environmental factors as well in the development of ports situated in major urban areas.
It is evident to all hon. members, I am sure, that reforms are long overdue. The reason for successive delays cannot be justified by this government. Greater decentralization must allow port profits to be invested in modernization and development of all international ports in Canada.
Continuing federal subsidies will be needed for smaller ports such as the port of Churchill, for example, that are essential to a region but that probably will never be able to achieve financial self-sufficiency. It is most important, as the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) said to me a few minutes ago, that a Canadian ports corporation set national policy to ensure that there is a co-ordinated and well integrated port strategy across Canada that takes into consideration the special needs of smaller less economically efficient ports.
Unlike some Conservative members who I believe are advocating complete privatization of our ports with no strings attached, we in the NDP believe that a national ports system should be co-ordinated federally while allowing maximum autonomy for local decision making.
The port of Vancouver makes a profit each year despite outdated facilities, facilities that have remained outdated because of National Harbours Board restrictions. Ottawa, under the National Harbours Board, at present continues to take away the gravy. It takes away the surplus funds. In fact, it generally controls the budget in the port of Vancouver. This has inhibited local development plans which cannot be implemented.
We believe that profits in the larger ports must be reinvested in port improvements in order for them to be competitive internationally. When these developments are completed and the financing or long-term capital plans are assured, surely then we can afford to share some of the surplus funds with other regions of Canada, but not under the scheme proposed in Bill C-92. We do not agree with the proposals in Bill C-92 which provide for continued federal control of budgets of local ports and which will still cream off surpluses which could forestall much needed port development and improvements. We, of course, Mr. Speaker, do agree with the concept of local autonomy for larger ports that are able to be self-sufficient now on in the near future. We believe this should be done within a co-ordinated national system. I must say we also agree with the last speaker, who has pointed out that we are not at all convinced that the Liberal minister and the Liberal government really believe in this, and certainly they have not spelled it out in detail to our satisfaction in Bill C-92. Therefore, there must be specific changes in this bill which will
Canada Ports Corporation Act
clarify the concept of decentralization and autonomy to the much greater satisfaction of local ports.
The port manager must have greater autonomy to make operational decisions under the direction of a local port operation without having to wait for approval from Ottawa. Currently a port authority must apply to the National Harbours Board through Treasury Board for capital expenditures up to $50,000, no more. Since one container crane costs $5 million, this is hardly realistic for most of the larger ports. Federal delays are intolerable.
The local port corporation also is the most logical port body to upgrade and modernize the port facility, and to be competitive within a particular region. There must be capital funds for long-range plans. In Vancouver, for example, we have a 20 to 30-year planning scheme being developed now with the municipalities, the provinces, the maritime unions, the businesses and adjacent communities, as well as with users of the ports. Users and regional bodies must be represented in the planning. These developments must be co-ordinated with multi-modal transport systems.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, I was amazed in Vancouver when I spoke to the port manager there at one time and learned that he did not know whom to contact in the railway system if there should be a major disaster in downtown Vancouver. He did not know the name of the person. There did not seem to be any intersystem kind of linkage that would assure the citizens, the city and the residents of our region, that we would not be blown up by some of the very dangerous cargoes that go through downtown Vancouver.
The capital funds for long-range plans must be assured, so that we can have reasonable planning. The local board must co-ordinate with the interprovincial and national policies and plans through the Canada Ports Corporation which will replace the National Harbours Board. This party agrees with the concept of local autonomy in port administration. We do feel that the government must be more explicit in terms of financial autonomy.
We do not agree with some of the other concepts which are implicit in this bill. It is indeed unfortunate that Members of Parliament are not allowed to discuss the regulations as well as the bill itself, since we fear that many of our concerns will be built into specific regulations, as the bill itself is very general in nature.
Our major concerns, Mr. Speaker, are in the following areas. First of all, there is the method of appointment to local port corporations, which will foster patronage, the typical way of developing ports on the part of the Liberal government, which allows no local or provincial appointees. We do not feel that regional advisory groups which are rather token in nature and do not have any real authority, are good enough to provide the input and the rational decentralized planning which is needed.

June 22, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
Secondly, there is the requirement that the local ports must be financially independent before they can achieve autonomy. This will impose a user-pay type of policy, which again is a favourite Liberal concept that will be penalizing and self-defeating for most ports in Canada which may not have a continuing high volume of business.
Thirdly, we are concerned about the lack of accountability to Parliament. This Parliament should be the body to decide when a local port corporation is applying to move for a change in category, for example, to become a harbour commission, in effect an independent Crown corporation. Under Bill C-92 this decision is made by orders in council with no reference to Parliament and no requirement for parliamentary sanction.
Wait ten years?

I would like to elaborate further on these points, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to hear from the minister afterwards.
As Sir Alexander Gibb said in 1932-and how apt it may be with regard to this bill if it goes through as planned:
Local ports should not be riddled with political patronage by the party in power.
This undoubtedly will happen if Bill C-92 is passed as it stands. If the minister recommends appointees to the board and the cabinet decides, I think we can all speculate on who is going to be on that board. We will recommend in committee that the structure and process of appointments to the local port corporation board must include greater accountability to the local region which is served by the port.
We agree that the port board members must be experts who are knowledgeable about port operations. It should not just be anyone. We can have political patronage at the local level as well. It is particularly important that experienced workers be appointed to the boards, locally and nationally.
Hear, hear!

I met with the CLC Committee which involves all waterfront unions, and this certainly is their opinion. We also agree that token appointments by city council or municipalities of just any old local alderman is not the way to go. We will press for a revised structure which will allow municipalities to recommend qualified people to the local port corporations board, as well as candidates who are proposed by maritime unions, local businesses, and the province, with a minority of federal appointees to be added. It is essential that the board members reflect diverse local interests and are not just defeated Liberal candidates.
Hear, hear!

We also feel that local board chairpersons should be voting members of the national board, not just exofficio members. What is the point in having a national harbours board simply with token liaison persons from the local board? We feel that they must be voting members of the national board. The local port authority must be required to
plan in a co-ordinated way with the municipalities and adjacent communities on matters such as access roads, traffic problems, movement of dangerous goods, environmental concerns as well as recreational access to the waterfront and port activities. Why should should children, for example, not be able to go and see at first hand the workings of the port? Why should our citizens who live near the port not have open access to the waterfront of the port? It should not be only the more affluent people who have access to beaches and waterfront areas.
Another question is that of financial self-sufficiency. As a Vancouver member, I agree that the port of Vancouver must be autonomous and financially self-sufficient with powers to reinvest the surplus in developments that are needed. This is necessary not only for the Vancouver region but for all of Canada, as this port is vital to the economy of Canada.
Our party also is just as concerned about the total port system in Canada and particularly about the less affluent and northern regions where financial self-sufficiency is an impossible dream. We are also concerned about ports like that of Prince Rupert, which is of interest to the member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton).
Hear, hear!
This is the fastest growing port in Canada and it deserves local autonomy, even though at this time it does not have the huge profit and needs much development to make it the port of the future.
That is right. Let us hear more about that.

There are also many activities going on to my left, Mr. Speaker. Just as we opposed a laid-on user-pay system for Canadian National Railways and other transportation systems in Canada, we oppose user-pay policy for our ports. Our national transportation system in Canada, a country so large and diverse, simply cannot be seen as just another business which can be operated only on a user-pay concept.
