While these bills were not perfect, they would have initiated greater change and would have provided more local autonomy than the bill we are dealing with today.
In his speech on June 14, the minister stated that, "We must have the best ports policy we can muster." I agree wholeheartedly with that statement and I would like to inform him that the House has seen bills such as C-61, C-6 and C-50 which are better than Bill C-92. They would have provided more of the degree of local autonomy that the port of Vancouver so desperately needs. Bill C-50, Bill C-92's immediate predecessor, was introduced in the House on March 19, 1979. The inadequacies of Bill C-92 are glaring in comparison with Bill C-50. First of all, in Bill C-50, the transport minister, after Treasury Board consultation, can give direction on financial management, operating and capital budgets and evaluation of assets to a port commission. In Bill C-92, the local port corporations will be classified as Schedule C bodies-which I might add is not explicit in the bill either-and their operating and capital budgets must be approved by Treasury Board.
In Bill C-50, port commissions can receive initial working capital for a total aggregate not to exceed $98 million, and can receive working capital, repayable in one year, and total aggregate not to exceed $20 million. There is provision for cancellation of National Harbours Board debts up to $505 million, and some portion can be deemed as capital for a port commission. In C-92, the Canada Ports Commission and the local ports commissions can receive working capital, but the total aggregate for both cannot exceed $10 million. There is no provision for cancellation of any debt, and all liabilities are transferred to the local port corporations.
It has been done.

In Bill C-50, port commissions can make bylaws with cabinet approval. In Bill C-92, there is provision for cabinet to amend any bylaw of a local port corporation. There is less of interface in Bill C-50. Port commissions deal with the Canada Ports commissioner who implements the minister's responsibilities and directions, while local port corporations must deal with the minister and board of directors of the Canada Ports Corporation.
In Bill C-50, all substantial ports were to be proclaimed as port commissions by governor in council. In Bill C-92, a noncorporate port which wants to achieve the status of a local port corporation must receive the approval of the parent corporation, the minister and cabinet.
Canada Ports Corporation Act
In Bill C-50, the port commissions were to receive their powers automatically. In Bill C-92, it is up to the CPC to decide which powers to give a local port corporation. In Bill C-50, the Auditor General was to have been a joint auditor for the port commissions. There is no such provision in Bill C-92. Why? Is the minister afraid of having the Auditor General audit the books of the Canada Ports Corporation, and if he is not, why is it not there? It is not in the bill, again. In Bill C-50, port commissions-I could go on with this matter. I could go on and talk for an hour about it, but I do not really think it makes much sense for me to do so. I think I have indicated enough distaste, enough anger and enough annoyance with this deliberate attempt to centralize the port of Vancouver back here in Ottawa and the deliberate attempt, by the use of propaganda booklets, to convince the people of the west coast that it is a good thing, and none of it is in the bill.
Mr. Speaker, I think I will close on this note. I would like to state that the only way I would support this bill would be if the port of Vancouver were excluded from its provisions by amendment and if its status were changed to that of a harbour commission port.
They asked to be included.

If the Liberal Party cannot deliver on its leader's promise, then I ask that this bill be allowed to die and the question of marine policies of this country be addressed only to the Progressive Conservative Party when it may be returned to power.
How sad!

We have three Senators on the west coast, we have the apologizer, the fund-raiser and the sneaky Pete. All three of them out there are selling British Columbia, through this bill, down the river and the river happens to be the St. Lawrence.
You should go home occasionally.

I am not prepared to allow Ottawa to continue totally to decide our fate and to steal the profits which the port of Vancouver makes, without any recourse whatsoever. I warn my colleagues in the NDP and I warn hon. members of the House that when they go to the electorate in British Columbia again, let them remember that one of the things people will realize, because I will make sure they realize it, that if anyone votes for this ruddy bill, this rip-off of British Columbia, they will face the electorate on the basis that they voted to allow the central Canadian government of this country to steal the profits from the port of Vancouver and not to give the port of Vancouver any of the autonomy it so richly deserves and needs to operate in the 1980s.
It is a despicable bill, and I thank you, Sir.
Hear, hear!
I might run against you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
In introducing this bill, the minister clearly stated that he expected most National Harbours Board ports will be able to achieve local port co-operation status. Therefore, let us look at the powers of a local port corporation compared to
June 22, 1982

what the NHB ports have now. Let me give hon. members just a few examples of the new powers this bill would provide. First, port managers are now appointed by the National Elarbours Board in Ottawa. A local port corporation would have the power under this bill to appoint its own port manager.
That makes all the difference in the world.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
So, that is why I do not know why the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) is drawing in the red herring of patronage and everything else. The local port corporation will have this power to appoint its own port manager.
Second, rates and tariffs for services are now fixed by bylaw and are therefore subject to governor in council approval. Under Bill C-92, the local port corporation would set its own rates and tariffs with the single exception, of course, of harbour dues which will still be set by bylaw. Third, at present there is a $250,000 limit on spending for local projects and programs. Beyond that, Treasury Board approval is required, and we all know how long that process takes. Under the bill, much greater spending authority will be granted.
If funds for the proposed program are derived solely from working capital, that is not requiring government grants, then authority in the order of $5 million is being contemplated. Now there is a limit in legislation, as the hon. member who spoke before me mentioned, of $50,000 on the awarding of contracts. Again, a much greater limit is envisaged. In addition, any limit would be contained in bylaws rather than the legislation itself, so that changes can be made to fit future circumstances. The minister will be in a better position and will have more time to provide specifics when the bill reaches committee stage.
Finally, local port corporations will have clear authority over the employment of all persons necessary for the conduct of the affairs of the individual port. These examples clearly indicate a greater degree of autonomy. When the minister introduced the bill on June 14, he made it very clear that the ports had reached adulthood. The time has come to give them more freedom of operation than in the past.
The hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby referred to Bill C-50. A comparison with the predecessor to this bill, Bill C-50, shows that the degree of autonomy at the outset in perhaps not as great as in the present proposal. The minister made it very clear in his speech that the reason is that a balance had to be struck between the objectives of autonomy and accountability. The approach taken in this bill is one of evolution. It is quite possible that the degree of autonomy will be as great as in Bill C-50 over time, but the evolutionary process must take place.
This is because it will be possible to transfer from a Schedule C to a Schedule D Crown corporation without change to legislation. For the time being, ports will remain as Schedule C which, it should be recognized and I think hon. members recognize, has certain advantages. They do not have
Canada Ports Corporation Act
to pay any income tax. There are no dividends. They are eligible for government grants. Also, it will be possible to transfer to harbour commission status, the most autonomous of port structures in Canada.
I should add that this bill fulfills the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in January 1980 in Vancouver. The member for North Vancouver-Burnaby referred to that visit by the Prime Minister. I think the Prime Minister's promise has been fulfilled by this bill, that this government would give greater autonomy to the port of Vancouver, something I am sure the members from Vancouver would wish for their constituents.
In summary, I am convinced that the autonomy that will be achieved by individual ports through this bill will be very real. It is not just paying lip service. The changes are not cosmetic. Port communities across the country will applaud Members of Parliament in all parties for having supported this important piece of legislation.
Before closing, I would like to take a moment to commend the members of the Transport Committee for the way they worked together, sometimes in a very partisan fashion, but when the need arose for partisan politics to be set aside, they pushed through good legislation and good policies. If we can get this bill into committee, I know with that committee it will come out a much better and improved bill, something that Canadians right across Canada want.
I commend the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). When he spoke on the bill, he said:
We want this kind of legislation. It is constructive legislation ... The minister knows I personally want to see this bill through second reading, into committee and back into this chamber before we adjourn for the summer.
That is the kind of commitment and undertaking that Canadians want from the Official Opposition. The members in the gallery are listening to this. It has caught their attention. Members in opposition have a role to play, as do members on this side. The members on the Transport Committee are not pushed around. They know what they want. They know what is good for Canadians. I know that they will put this bill through and it will come out an excellent bill in the long run.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin my remarks on Bill C-92, which enacts the Canada Ports Corporation Act by considering the main thrust of the new part of this legislation. The two major features of this bill are, First, the establishment of a national ports policy and, second, the creation of a new corporate structure or framework to permit implementation of that policy.
If the national ports policy is sound and sensible and the organizational structure is efficient and effective, the bill will be a forward step for Canada's marine transportation industry. However, there is a real danger that a deficient ports policy and an inefficient and ineffective organizational structure will not be quickly or easily remedied. Indeed, it has taken over 45 years and three false starts in the House of Commons to produce Bill C-92. The warning and the challenge are both

June 22, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
clear. We must examine the provisions of Bill C-92, particularly the new ports policy and the new organizational structure with a critical but open mind.
If on balance the new legislative provisions have merit, the bill ought to proceed to the appropriate committee for close and detailed examination. However, if the provisions contain defects that cannot be rectified or remedied, we ought to recognize that the eventual enactement of Bill C-92 will wreak havoc on a delicate but viable national ports system. For this reason, we should examine the current scope and status of the national harbours system in the context of the total marine transportation system.
First let me explain what I mean by the marine transportation system. It is an integrated system of onshore facilities and marine vessels coupled with the land transportation system that allows cargo to flow internationally and across Canada and to other points of destination.
Canada is very much involved in international trade. As the minister mentioned when he made his remarks on second reading of Bill C-92 on June 14, 1982, the 15 national ports handle 50 per cent of the cargo that flows across all Canadian ports and port facilities. That is 80 per cent of the total exports that Canada delivers to points beyond its boundaries.
It is very easy to see what is the force and effect of our port system. It handles the great bulk of export cargo and is very much a part of our international transportation system.
1 commend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) for allowing that international flavour to continue to exist in our marine transportation system. If he were to take the attitude of his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) who looks upon the petroleum industry as something that can be Canadianized, other international participants being excluded, we would have havoc in marine transportation in Canada and in its interconnections with international associations. There is within this national ports policy the capability to continue the international connections that have existed since time immemorial in Canada. We will be able to take part in a national transportation system to the benefit of all parts of Canada as well as to the benefit of our trading partners, and to the benefit of participation in international trade. That is something that must be kept in mind as part of the larger world. If we exclude ourselves from that it will be to the detriment of the whole of the nation.
Let me look at the structure of the National Harbours Board as it exists today. We have the central authority, we want to have it decentralized. I would remind members of the House that that act of decentralization has already been started. In fact, many of the positions and many of the divisions and many of the internal structures that are part of the National Harbours Board complex have already been decentralized. So there has been taking place within the structures of the National Harbours Board a degree of decentralization and to some extent some of the ports like the port of Halifax have experienced that kind of decentralized control. So in
many ways it exists throughout the national port system. I am referring primarily to the 15 national ports that are distinguishable from the harbours commission ports and the ports that are merely operated under the Government Piers and Harbours Act. There does exist with respect to some of those 15 ports a kind of local autonomy. I think those ports, like the port of Halifax, that have had a degree of local autonomy, realize and recognize that this is a very viable kind of control and that if it is increased and advanced in the future it may have traumatic effects on the ability of local ports to service their communities and to create greater economic opportunities within those coastal communities.
One thing we should keep in mind, however, Mr. Speaker, is the competition that already exists amongst national ports that operate under the National Harbours Board at present. That competition, Mr. Speaker, in many ways can be quite healthy but in other ways may be quite damaging. Just as evidence that such competition exists, I refer to an article by Mr. Charles N. Forward, entitled "The Development of Canada's Five Leading National Ports". I hasten to add that included in that designation of five leading national ports are the ports of Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax, as well as the port of Vancouver. Of course, the first four named ports are on the east coast of Canada and are in direct competition. Mr. Forward says in his article:
Competition between the ports has waxed and waned throughout the years and specific regional rivalries have developed. Montreal and Quebec have competed for the trade focused on the St. Lawrence system, as have Halifax and Saint John for that focused on the ice-free Atlantic coast. But in a broader context, Montreal and Quebec have co-operated against their Atlantic rivals in defending the St. Lawrence share of national trade versus that of the Atlantic ports.
What that statement makes clear, Mr. Speaker, is that the ports of Montreal and Quebec, with the assistance of the national structure that exists in the National Harbours Board, have combined their efforts to take an unfair advantage of the east coast ports of Halifax and St. John. Nobody knows that better than the participants in port activity in the port of Halifax. They have always seen the Montreal-Quebec complex as being unfair competition. Whether that statement can be documented in terms of statistics over the years hardly matters, because the perception is very clear. The federal authority, through the National Harbours Board, has given unfair advantage to the ports in Quebec, and particularly the port of Montreal.
What example can I give, Mr. Speaker, of unfair advantage? There are allegations of sweetheart deals in the port of Montreal, given by the National Harbours Board through its local officers, to companies and to onshore companies which operate vessels, like the TASK group that maintain facilities and utilize the port of Montreal. How can that allegation be countered? Very simply, Mr. Speaker, by producing the facts that relate to these deals that exist in the port of Montreal and in all the national ports under the control of the National Harbours Board.
Is that kind of information forthcoming, Mr. Speaker? No, Sir, there is litigation before the courts right now, where the
June 22, 1982

litigating parties are asking for this information. Mr. Speaker, Halterm, which operates the major container terminal in the port of Halifax, has had an increase in its rental fees, at the demand of the National Harbours Board, from 15 cents a square foot to 65 cents a square foot. Naturally, Mr. Speaker, the operators of that tremendous container facility in the port of Halifax want to know if this is a fair increase in the rental for the facilities they have. They can only know that if they know what their competitors are paying in the port of Montreal and the port of Quebec and other ports operating under the same National Harbours Board system. That information is not provided, so they do now know, and thus the suspicions rise. So, Mr. Speaker, it is important that we recognize what has been happening in the current set up through the National Harbours Board. We have the competition between the ports, particularly the ports on the east coast. We have that competition based on what may be unfair practices, in terms of sweetheart deals for rental facilities at less than their value.
1 would remind members of this House, Mr. Speaker, that the National Harbours Board in its last report, for 1981, had a net income of $59.8 million, and that was on total revenues of only $180 million. So, Mr. Speaker, the National Harbours Board is doing very well through the ports that it now operates, the national ports like Halifax and St. John's. We have to be very wary, Mr. Speaker, to be sure that the National Harbours Board is administering the act fairly among the ports under its jurisdiction.
There is another point that we have to put on the record in this House, so that we can properly judge this bill and judge whether it is going to remedy the mischief that has occurred in the past. 1 refer to the recent write-off of debts by the National Harbours Board with the aid and co-operation of the Government of Canada. That write-off amounted to something like $475 million. The Minister of Transport recently in the House quoted an amount of $500 million, which is even greater. That write-off of debt consisted of $350 million of capital debt and $150 million in interest on that capital debt. That debt of $500 million that is owed by the National Harbours Board to the government and to the people of Canada was simply wiped out. But how is it wiped out and in respect of what ports was it wiped out? Well, $133 million in capital and $98 million in interest was wiped out, cleared off the books, cancelled, in respect of the port of Montreal. So, Mr. Speaker, there we have $231 million of debt wiped out in the case of the port of Montreal. That is over half of the total debt write-off. When you do things like that, Mr. Speaker, it is not hard to realize that this great national organization called the National Harbours Board can show a net income of $59.8 million. But the taxpayers of Canada should not be fooled by this, because there is no $59.8 million in real net income terms. It is simply $59.8 million taken from one pocket of the taxpayers and put into another pocket of the government and a government agency. So, Mr. Speaker, we have to be very wary.
I wanted to point out, before I get to more positive remarks about the bill, that we do have a few complaints about the
Adjournment Debate
National Harbours Board, we do have a few complaints about the way the government has dealt with the National Harbours Board and with the way the National Harbours Board has dealt with some of the national ports, particularly the port of Halifax, in debt write-off and in the matter of creation of facilities.
There is a great deal more, Mr. Speaker, that I want to say, but if I might call it ten o'clock and resume the debate at a future time, I would be quite happy to do so.

subtopic: FARM CREDIT CORPORATION-AVAILABILITY OF FUNDING. (B) ADVANCE CROP PAYMENTS
FARM CREDIT CORPORATION-AVAILABILITY OF FUNDING. (B) ADVANCE CROP PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about two weeks ago I had an opportunity to question the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in this House during question period concerning items very important to the agricultural community in Canada. I asked about plans that the government may or may not have for assisting farmers in financing their day-to-day affairs. Specifically I referred to some of the things the government could be doing now as the result of the passage of Bill C-88, dealing with farm credit, that enables the Farm Credit Corporation to raise money by any means, with the concurrence of the Minister of Finance.
I asked the Minister of Finance about plans he may or may not have to support the Minister of State in the other place, who is responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), in their efforts to raise the level of cash advance under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. Specifically, I was concerned about what the government intended to do with the Farm Credit Corporation.
As the farmers of this country know, for a long time the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) promised that the Farm Credit Corporation would receive additional funds with which to enable farmers to meet their financial commitments. Many times over the past few months, prior to June 1, the minister has made the statement that the corporation would receive an additional $1 billion in funds on June 1 that would be available for loans to farmers at favourable interest rates. Many members of the agriculture committee which dealt with Bill C-88
18790

June 22, 1982
Adjournment Debate
thought that the minister was going to make use of Clause 16 of the bill which reads as follows:
The Corporation may, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, borrow money by any means, including issuing and selling bonds, debentures, notes and other evidences of indebtedness of the Corporation.
To a lot of members that meant that the corporation was going to be in a position, with the concurrence of the Minister of Finance, to make use of the small business bond which had worked quite well during the two years it was in operation and before the Minister of Finance changed it in the budget of November 12, 1981.
If the Minister of Agriculture can prevail upon the Minister of Finance to allow the Farm Credit Corpration to make use of some of those areas of the bill that would allow the Farm Credit Corporation to raise money, it would be of assistance to the farming community.
Members of this party have often suggested that the agribond concept be adopted. This would mean that a farmer would have the opportunity to lend money to the Farm Credit Corporation at a preferred rate of interest and would likely do so, if he was assured that the money would be made available to farmers or people engaged in agriculture in his own area in order to assist them with their ventures.
This is important to the farming community, because farming has become very productive in the past few years due to the fact that it is increasingly capital intensive. This means that more money is needed to finance the day-to-day operations of the farm. Anything we can do to assist farmers to gain access to financing at reasonable rates will help them.
This is evident in present conditions of extremely high rates of interest. The books of many farm operations show that the largest single cost is not in relation to seed, fertilizers, repairs or wages, but interest payments. This situation puts a strain on the farming community's efforts to remain as productive as it has been in the past. This is a very serious matter and the Minister of Finance should pursue it. I hope the parliamentary secretary will respond favourably tonight to the suggestion I put forward in my question two weeks ago.
The second thing that I want to cover is what is happening to the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. The purpose of this act was to enable the Canadian Wheat Board to make advances to farmers who have grains, handled by the board; wheat, oats or barley, in storage; that is, to borrow money against them. The money is not in the form of a gift, but simply an advance against the grain that has been grown but not yet marketed. The loan is interest free; the federal government picks up the interest. That provision has been widely used in the past. The act went into effect in 1957.
At that time the limit on the advance was $5,000. Subsequently, it was raised to $15,000. But that can only be a portion of the money represented by his stored grain. As an example, if a farmer only grew $10,000 worth of grain, he would not be able to obtain a $15,000 cash advance. He could obtain approximately two-thirds of the initial price, which
would work out to probably something like 50 per cent of the value of the grain. So it simply means that once a farmer has grown the grain and stored it, if he is not able to sell it he can go to the Canadian Wheat Board, get a cash advance and use that as normal operating funds to pay for fertilizer, seed and other operating expenses.
This has been very useful, Mr. Speaker, but I have two statistics which point out what has happened as interest rates have gone up and farmers, like any other businessmen in the country, have found themselves in a cost-price squeeze. In 1980 there were something like 15,400 applications. In 1981 that number almost doubled to 28,000. But the interesting fact is that in 1980 there was something like $61 million advanced to farmers under this act, but in 1981, even though the number of farmers did not quite double, the amount of money loaned out went up by three times, to over $205 million. That gives you some idea of the use of that provision by farmers.
I suggest that if the government is interested we on this side would co-operate and put through an amendment to the bill which would substantially raise the level from $15,000. I do not know what the figure should be, but I suggest it should be $25,000 or $30,000 at least. There have been suggestions that it go to $50,000. If the government did that, farmers would have access to additional funding for the beginning of the crop year, which is August 1. I hope the parliamentary secretary will respond favourably to those two suggestions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FARM CREDIT CORPORATION-AVAILABILITY OF FUNDING. (B) ADVANCE CROP PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has asked the minister to take a look at some of his ideas, and I personally welcome them as concrete suggestions. I may say in return that the hon. member must know that the minister, as he showed today, has quite a few ideas of his own and we are all looking forward to his announcements next week. We will hope that we can have additional discussions on this in the future.
The minister is aware of the financial difficulties faced by many farmers, and he is examining new measures being proposed to provide selective aid to those farmers with viable operations but who are in financial distress. The member has mentioned the question of an extra $1 billion for funding the Farm Credit Corporation. I refer him to Bill C-88 which was proclaimed on April 8 this year. It provides for an extra $75 million in government equity in the FCC, and that amount in turn increases the corporation's statutory borrowing authority by an additional $1,875,000. Amendments to the act also enable the FCC to borrow funds externally with approval of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), and this provides a more flexible source of financing, the use of which is currently being studied by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the FCC. Initially it would, of course, be unreasonable to expect the FCC to borrow $ 1 billion as its first venture into the private sector.
Bill C-88 also provides for interest rebates of 5 per cent over
two years under the $45 million special loan program designed
to assist farmers in financial distress.
June 22, 1982

The hon. member has referred to the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. An amendment to provide additional funding is under consideration. However, the hon. member suggests that additional funding could be made available to farmers under this program without increasing the deficit. He should know that advances under that act are made to farmers by the Canadian Wheat Board using its line of credit with chartered banks, guaranteed by the Minister of Finance under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. The government pays the cost of interest and is liable for any loss which may occur in the event of a default.
The hon. member should know that in the year ended March 31, 1982, payments in connection with the Prairie Grains Advance Payments Act totalled some $13 million as was reported to this House in the final supplementary estimates for that year.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT ACID RAIN SUBCOMMITTEE BE REACTIVATED
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT ACID RAIN SUBCOMMITTEE BE REACTIVATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see that my good friend, the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Gimaiel) is here this evening. We served together on the acid rain subcommittee. Acid rain is the subject of my remarks tonight. I want everyone to know, hon. members and anyone who is listening or watching these proceedings, that the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean and others serving on that committee came down with a unanimous report on the terrible urgency for this country and the United States to do something jointly about the acid rain problem.
What is significant is that the all-party subcommittee on acid rain worked extraordinarily well together. All of us believed, no matter what our partisan political position, that Canada is being hammered to death by acid rain, as is the United States although not proportionately to the same degree. However, certain places in the United States are taking just as much punishment.
Our subcommittee agreed jointly and in a non-partisan way that something had to be done about acid rain. We had the unique advantage of being able to go to Americans and say, "One of the differences you have in this country is the acid rain situation." On this subject there was no partisan difference among the major political parties of our country. Acid rain has to be stopped. We cannot stop acid rain all by ourselves. Fifty per cent of the acid rain that falls on Canada comes from the United States and 50 per cent comes from us. But the only way to stop acid rain is by having a joint agreement. The hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean, along with many members of all parties, who know exactly what I am talking about, will not disagree-I hope they will not disagree-with anything I have to say tonight.
In recent days we have seen headlines in newspapers. There was a report in The Globe and Mail on Wednesday, June 16, 1982, which stated that the U.S. blames the stalling of talks on acid rain was as a consequence of statements made by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) for the Government of Canada. The minister is saying effectively that the Americans do not want an agreement-at least the American
Adjournment Debate
administration does not want an agreement. There is a big difference there because this does not apply to all Americans. The American administration does not want an agreement and is stalling. That is what the minister is saying.
Hon. members know that on June 17, the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan), my colleague in the Conservative Party and spokesman for environmental affairs for our party, raised the following question with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau): "Please, will you get involved in this in a much more high profile way?" On the same day I put a question to the Right Hon. Prime Minister, asking him to please reactivate the subcommittee on acid rain. The Prime Minister said he would take those remarks under consideration and pass them on to the Minister of Environment.
On June 16, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), a member of the New Democratic Party who served on our acid rain subcommittee, moved a motion under Standing Order 43, asking that the government reactivate the subcommittee on acid rain. A day later 1 put questions to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) asking what response his department has given to the subcommittee's unanimous report that was brought down last October on what must be done to stop acid rain in this country and in the United States. I am sorry to say that the Minister of Energy said he had discussions occasionally with the Minister of the Environment, but the Minister of Energy did not answer my question about what kind of response in writing that department had given.
I must tell hon. members that we are in a very, very serious situation. The Minister of the Environment is not mincing words when he says that these talks with the Americans are in imminent danger of collapse. I urge all hon. members to join with me tonight in endorsing the necessity to reactivate the acid rain subcommittee.
This is not the first time this has been requested. I wrote a letter to the Minister of the Environment on May 12, 1981, asking that the acid rain subcommittee not be disbanded. On June 5, 1981, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Irwin), who was the chairman of our very effective committee and who gave great service to the country and to the committee-and I do not apologize for saying that-also wrote to the hon. House leader asking, "Please don't disband the acid rain committee."
Recently the Minister of the Environment spoke to the Air Pollution Control Association in New Orleans on June 21, 1982. By the way, I was invited by that group some number of weeks ago to participate in a special seminar on air pollution problems in North America. At that time the minister said:
In Canada we are deeply disappointed with the state of negotiations between my country and the United States government on acid rain. The footdragging and interference in the development of scientific information has reached frustrating proportions. The administration's rejection of our proposal to reduce sulphur dioxide emissions in eastern North America by 50 per cent by 1990 and

June 22, 1982
Adjournment Debate
a clear indication that it may be some considerable period of time before it will be able even to begin to discuss control actions, is a bitter pill for us to swallow.
In the moment or two remaining I want to say that if we are to win this battle, we must break away from traditional diplomatic channel because they are not sufficient. I see the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean nodding in agreement. We have been through this and we know that we must find other ways to get at American legislators. We need to reactivate the acid rain subcommittee. We need to have Members of Parliament from all parties going to the members of the House of Representatives and to American senators. We need to support our own Canadian coalition against acid rain. We need to have individuals working under a policy to co-ordinate and support the efforts of hundreds of thousands of Americans who also want to stop acid rain in their country.
My question is simple. It arises out of the questions which I and other members have put in the House and through correspondence. Will the government consider reactivating the subcommittee on acid rain to give us a chance to get at American legislators? I know, because I have been there, as have other members, that we can get to them on a personal basis. That is not possible through traditional diplomatic channels. We must use every possible resource, tactic and strategic, available to us. If we do not do that, I say that we will fail in this. We cannot have a quarter of our country savaged by this terrible phenomenon because it will not be accepted by our children or our children's children.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT ACID RAIN SUBCOMMITTEE BE REACTIVATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to respond to the question of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser). The fact-finding report of the subcommittee on acid rain has been helpful in raising public awareness of the acid rain issue in both Canada and the United States.
A number of the recommendations of the subcommittee form part of the program activities which we have been carrying out for some time. To note just a few, in April, 1981, Environment Canada issued national emission guidelines for new thermal power plants. A review of new motor vehicle emission standards for nitrous oxide is underway. Standardized monitoring techniques are being put in place. United States legislators and journalists have visited Canada to see our concerns first hand.
The hon. member for Vancouver South quoted from the minister's speech in New Orleans. I should like to continue that quotation, wherein the minister said:
The latest obstacles, which occurred less than one week ago at a negotiating session in Ottawa, are forcing us to an agonizing reappraisal of the usefulness of continuing discussions.
He continued:
Our emission reduction proposal was drawn from the same science that U.S. negotiators have drawn diametrically opposed conclusions. On a per capita basis our proposal is more costly to Canadians than to Americans. We are willing to put our money where our mouth is. I can only conclude that the values and factors influencing Canadian decision-making are considerably different from those in the U.S.
Acid rain remains one of our foremost environmental problems. We are looking for ways to break the log jam, to continue constructive dialogue with the United States to find solutions to this problem. This is important since in Canada, as a whole, 50 per cent of our acid rain originates in the United States, and in the regions of particular concern, such as the tourist and recreation areas of Ontario, as much as 75 per cent of the acid rain comes from the United States.
When the sub-committee reported on the nature and complexity of the acid rain problem it concluded that the problem was indeed serious. The nature of several of its recommendations also clearly indicates that regardless of the complexity, enough is already known to begin taking control action. This position has been clearly accepted.
The minister is aware of the concern hon. members have expressed over the state of acid rain negotiations. He shares their frustration with the lack of progress that has been made so far. Indeed, he welcomes any suggestion which could help bring discussions with the U.S. to a fruitful conclusion.
As I mentioned earlier, the Department of Environment is currently undergoing a reassessment of its approach in these difficult negotiations. Reactivating the subcommittee is one of a variety of options which are available to the government. The suggestion and the interest of the hon. member is appreciated and will certainly be considered as a possible alternative to our current method of negotiation.
If the minister and the government decide that reactivation of the subcommittee may help resolve the serious problem of acid raid, this option will be given serious consideration. In any event, with the vast amount of knowledge that members of the subcommittee have accumulated, I would encourage them to continue making their views known so that we can continue keeping up the pressure on the United States.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-INQUIRY RESPECTING MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO HELP LEBANON
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-INQUIRY RESPECTING MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO HELP LEBANON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before coming to the issue I wish to raise this evening, I would like to say that I am in complete agreement with the last comments made by the hon. member for Vancouver-South (Mr. Fraser) concerning acid rain. He has my full support and I hope that his representations will bring results.
As for the issue I want to raise myself, I directed a question this week to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) concerning the opportunities available to Lebanese people wishing to come to Canada because of the war in their own country. I asked to bring up this issue again, Mr. Speaker, because I want people in Canada to be better informed about the situation in Lebanon and the reasons why Canada should now help the Lebanese people.
As Canadians, we have some responsibility in this matter.
For two years, I have been trying to explain this responsibility
June 22, 1982

in the House, but it has not always been easy because the problem is very complex. I shall now try in the few minutes available to me to explain this responsibility. Hon. members will know that, for whatever reason, 40,000 Syrian soldiers have been residing in Lebanon for the last six years. Even though they were once invited into the country, these 40,000 Syrian soldiers constitute a foreign military force in Lebanon.
1 wish to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that Lebanon has always been an ally of Canada and of the western block, a capitalistic country, one of the most beautiful countries in the Middle East and of all the countries in the Middle East, the one which probably resembles most Canada. This has therefore been the situation in that country for the past six years. For two years, I have been asking the Canadian government to take a stand and to request that Syria withdraw its troops from Lebanon because, as everyone knows, the Lebanese people and the Palestinians, or the PLO for those who prefer, have been living together for years with no problem at all. There would be no problem if they were allowed to live together under a Lebanese government or under the supervision of a United Nations international force. These people are able to live together. The problem came about because the fact that a small country such as Lebanon, which has a population of 1.5 million, also included with its borders 40,000 Syrian soldiers as well as 300,000 Palestinians ten per cent of whom are armed to the teeth, in addition to all the weapons which enter the country regularly. This has created a kind of channel which was bringing war to the very borders of Israel, and for the last two years, I have stated frankly in this place for everyone to hear that Israel eventually would have no other choice but to attack Lebanon because of this enormous concentration of troups. This is the responsibility that Canada must share with all other western countries, Mr. Speaker. Since 1975, we have closed our eyes to the fact that Lebanon was bound to be the place where a war between other countries would be fought. Now, everyone is surprised to see that the Israelis and the Syrians are not bombing each other and are waging war on a territory which is not theirs. Not a single Israeli bomb as fallen on Syria and not a single Syrian bomb has fallen on Israel. These bombs fall on the country which is most similar to ours, our greatest friend in the Middle East, namely Lebanon.
In that context, considering that those people are being bombarded and that they are about to lose their homes, their wealth, their children and perhaps even their nationality, are we Canadians along with some of our allies such as the United States helping them today to find a way out of this predicament, or at least helping them to survive? I would ask the parliamentary secretary to further explain what he said this week. What does it mean for the Lebanese who are already here and for the others who are anxious to come to Canada, and what facilities will our government make available to them? I also wish that once and for all Canada would ask that all foreign troops be withdrawn from Lebanon, be they Syrians or Israelis. I also urge our government to support the Lebanese people as a nation and help them survive as a country, either by sending troops to join the UN forces or by voting in favour
Adjournment Debate
of maintaining there a military international peacekeeping force. But indeed we should let the Lebanese people be Lebanese, we should let that friendly country survive and be our friend. Mr. Speaker, I thank you for giving me those few minutes to make my point and I look forward to hearing the reply of the parliamentary secretary.

speakeroldname: Mr. Remi Bujold (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-INQUIRY RESPECTING MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO HELP LEBANON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first commend the honourable member for Lac-Saint-Jean for his contribution this evening and his plea for the Lebanese people. He showed an excellent knowledge of the situation in that country and his involvement in this issue for more than two years. It is true that Lebanon is going through extremely grave and trying times, and for that reason and to reply to all the points raised by the honourable member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Gimaiel) and others across the country, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) last week, on Tuesday June the 15th to be exact, announced the special measures taken by the Canadian government to face that most unfortunate situation now prevailing in Lebanon. I would like to take a few minutes to review those measures and try to bring them in better perspective for the benefit of Canadians. First, Mr. Speaker, the 1,000 visa holding Lebanese visitors now in Canada will be authorized to remain in Canada for one year after their visas have expired, in addition to that extension, a work permit will be granted. At the end of the one-year period, each individual case will be reviewed and a decision taken as to the possibility of applying for permanent resident status.
Second, Mr. Speaker, Lebanese visitors now in Canada and having close relatives in this country can, under the Act, apply for permanent resident status without having to leave the country in order to submit their applications outside of Canada.
Third, Mr. Speaker, Canadians or permanent Canadian residents with relatives facing difficulties in Lebanon will be entitled to sponsor the latter, even though they may not meet the usual criteria under the Immigration Act.
Fourth, Mr. Speaker, no person under a deportation order will be deported from Canada and sent back to Lebanon before the situation in that country is back to normal. It should be emphasized that it is difficult if not impossible to tell Beirut residents that for the time being no one can have access to our Canadian embassy. Just this evening, we saw on the newscast the bombing in Lebanon, especially in Beirut, and it is absolutely impossible to ensure that our Canadian embassy in Lebanon can extend usual services.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would emphasize that the Canadian government gave the International Red Cross SI million to help and support people now in Lebanon. Of

June 22, 1982

course, other steps will be considered in due time, and hopefully the situation in Lebanon will correct itself, and that friendly nation will be able once again to enjoy peace.
